RC circuit transients change as frequency changes. How they change is an important principle that relates to many circuits.
Using an oscilloscope, these waveforms can be observed while the frequency is varied.
In this lesson, you will observe the effects of a differentiating circuit (short time constant) on a square wave.
You will also observe the effects of an integrating circuit (long time constant) on a squarewave.
Let's begin the lesson on RC CIRCUIT TRANSIENT EXPERIMENT...................
. The experiment in this lesson is not setup to use the selected trainer.

This experiment demonstrates RC circuit transients. You will apply a square wave frequency to an RC circuit and observe the voltage and current waveforms for the capacitor. Next, you will vary the input frequency and predict the effects...
Pick up the PC130-14A card. This card contains four series RC circuits. Switches S1 - S4 select which circuit(s) the input is applied to.
The function generator is used to supply a DC square wave to the inputs.
Each circuit, A through D, has a different RC time constant. You will use circuit B. Let's start the experiment.
1. Set the Test Console controls to the initial control settings..........
2. Carefully plug PC130-14A into the Test Console PC1 position. ernal program = SCAN FCC 0 External program = SCAN PWR 0 1
3. Set switches S1, S3, and S4 to OUT (Left) on the PC130-14A. 4. Set switch S2 to IN (Right) on PC130-14A. ternal program = SCAN FTR 0 C1 00
MEASUREMENT SETUP - Place S1, S3 and S4 to OUT (left). Place S2 to IN (right).
5. Set the function generator for 1000 Hz square wave output. Be sure all modulation and attenuation controls are out..

With 1 kHz applied to circuit B, what do you predict the voltage waveform across the capacitor looks like?
Let's measure the voltage waveform across the capacitor and verify that it is indeed as you predicted.
Measuring voltage with an oscilloscope across a component that does not have either side connected to ground requires special procedures.
Since voltage is actually "difference of potential", the voltage across C2 is the difference of the voltage at TP4 and the voltage at TP5.
Since the oscilloscope has two channels, CH1 can measure the voltage at TP4 and CH2 can measure the voltage at TP5.
Using the ADD function and inverting CH2 of the oscilloscope subtracts CH2 from CH1. This displays the difference of TP4 and TP5 or Ec.
Trigger - CH1, AC, + Display Mode - ADD CH1 Volt/Div - 1 CH1 - GND

Notice the capacitor fully charges and fully discharges. The waveform is identical to time constant curves for charge and discharge of a capacitor.
What do you predict the current waveform through the capacitor looks like?
The current waveform through C2 shows complete charge and discharge curves in opposite directions.
Let's measure the current waveform through C2 and verify that it agrees with your prediction.
Since oscilloscopes cannot directly measure current, the voltage waveform across a resistor represents the current in a series circuit.
Since current is E/R, and current is in phase across a resistor, the Er and Ic waveshapes are the same.
6. Place the CH2 probe to TP5. The oscilloscope display indicates the current waveform through C2.
The top of the waveform represents charging current in one direction and the bottom shows discharge current in the opposite direction.
Compare the voltage across the capacitor with the current through it. Notice Ic is an AC waveform.
Current reverses direction when the capacitor stops charging and begins to discharge.
Let's see how current and voltage are affected when the input frequency is decreased. The time constant is short when compared with the time for Ea.
Remember, short time constants are used for differentiating circuits causing sharp pulses of Ic (voltage across R2).
2. Set the function generator for a frequency of 200 Hz.
With 200 Hz applied to circuit B what do you predict the voltage waveform across the capacitor will look like?
The voltage waveform across an RC circuit with a short time constant charges and discharges quickly.
Let's measure the voltage waveform across the capacitor and verify that it is as you predicted.

Notice the capacitor charges quickly compared to the long time for the applied voltage.
The flat tops and bottoms represent time when the capacitor is fully charged or discharged.
What do you predict the current waveform through the capacitor will look like?
The current waveform through C2 shows sharp pulses of Ic indicating a short RC time constant.
Let's measure the current waveform through C2 and verify that it agrees with your prediction.

6. Place the CH2 probe to TP5. The oscilloscope display indicates the current waveform through C2.
The sharp pulses show quick charge and discharge current while the "flat" zero point shows that current is zero when C2 is completely charged or discharged.
Compare the voltage across the capacitor with the current through it. Notice Ic changes only when there is a change in Ec.
Let's see how current and voltage are affected when the input frequency is increased. The time constant is long when compared with the time for the applied voltage.
Remember, long time constants cause Ec to rise and fall slowly, these are called integrating circuits.
2. Set the function generator for a frequency of 10 kHz.
With 10 kHz applied to circuit B, what do you predict the voltage waveform across the capacitor will look like?
The voltage waveform across an RC circuit with a long time constant charges and discharges slowly.
Let's measure the voltage waveform across the capacitor and verify that the waveform is as you predicted.

7. Place CH2 probe to TP5. The oscilloscope display indicates the voltage waveform across C2.
OSCILLOSCOPE LEAD PLACEMENT - Carefully connect CH2 probe to TP5.
Notice the slow charge and discharge of C2. With the input frequency high, C2 has very little time to charge and discharge.
Remember, the input squarewave is from +2V to 0V, an average DC level of 1V. Notice the 1V DC level the signal is riding on.
The capacitor drops the DC while passing most of the AC. The AC is dropped across R2.
What do you predict the current waveform through the capacitor will look like?
The current waveform through C2 shows high charge and discharge current, decreasing only slightly as C2 begins to take on a charge or to discharge.
Let's measure the current waveform through C2 and verify that it agrees with your prediction.

6. Place the CH2 probe to TP5. The oscilloscope display indicates the current waveform through C2.
Compare the voltage across C2 with the current through it. Notice Ic drops only slightly because C2 charges and discharges only a small amount.
This experiment has shown the effects on RC transient circuits by varying the input frequency.
